Three stages, three different skills

Prelims filters, Mains ranks, and the interview assesses suitability for public service.

GS-I decides the cutoff. CSAT is qualifying, but it now demands regular timed preparation—not last-week practice. Failure in CSAT eliminates the attempt; Prelims marks do not enter final merit.

Prepare your Detailed Application Form, current issues, balanced views, ethical dilemmas and clear communication. Never bluff.

The qualifying-language rule can cancel your Mains evaluation

Paper A (one Indian language) and Paper B (English) are 300 marks each, qualifying, and require at least 25% in each paper. If you miss the minimum in either paper, UPSC does not take cognizance of—or evaluate—the Essay, GS and Optional papers for ranking.

Paper A pattern: comprehension, précis writing, usage and vocabulary, short essays, plus translation from English to the chosen Indian language and vice versa. It is matriculation-standard, but needs timed practice.

Paper A is not compulsory for candidates hailing from Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Sikkim. Apply the exact exemption wording in the 2027 notification to your case.

Before applying

Use the new application workflow

The old One Time Registration (OTR) module is discontinued. Complete Account Creation → Universal Registration → Common Application Form in advance on UPSC’s new online portal, then the exam-specific section during the application window. Follow the application link in the 2027 notification on upsc.gov.in.

Application fee

₹100 for the application

Women and candidates belonging to SC, ST or PwBD categories are exempt. Always check the 2027 notice for payment windows and accepted modes.

After Prelims

DAF-I, then DAF-II

Qualified candidates submit DAF-I before Mains. Those called for the Personality Test submit DAF-II before interview; entries shape document checks and questions.

Eligibility shortcut: a recognised bachelor’s degree is required. General-category candidates are typically 21–32 years with 6 attempts; relaxations apply by category. Treat this only as orientation—read the 2027 notification before applying.

GS study notes

Read one subject, close it, and reproduce the framework from memory. These notes cover the durable concepts that repeatedly anchor Prelims and Mains questions.

04A

Polity & Constitution

Institutions · rights · federalism · governance

Constitutional architecture

  • The Constitution draws authority from “We, the People”. The Preamble states the republic’s objectives; it is part of the Constitution but is not an independent source of power.
  • Fundamental Rights in Part III are enforceable by courts. Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs; Article 226 gives High Courts a wider writ jurisdiction, including “for any other purpose”.
  • Directive Principles in Part IV are non-justiciable but fundamental in governance. Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA.
  • Article 368 governs most amendments. Some need a special parliamentary majority; changes affecting specified federal provisions also need ratification by at least half of the states.

Parliament and executive

  • The President is the constitutional head; the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister aids and advises. The Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
  • A Money Bill is defined by Article 110, can be introduced only in Lok Sabha, and reaches Rajya Sabha for recommendations; it must return it within 14 days. The Speaker certifies a Money Bill.
  • Parliamentary control works through questions, committees, debates, motions and financial approval. Department-related standing committees examine demands for grants and Bills in depth.

Federalism and accountability

  • Legislative subjects are divided through Union, State and Concurrent Lists. Residuary legislative power rests with Parliament.
  • The Comptroller and Auditor General under Article 148 audits public finances; the Finance Commission under Article 280 recommends tax devolution and grants.
  • Local self-government gained constitutional status through the 73rd and 74th Amendments. Devolution of functions, finances and functionaries determines real autonomy.
Recall frame: source of power → institution → appointment → tenure/removal → function → accountability → current issue.

History

Ancient · medieval · modern · freedom struggle

Ancient and early medieval India

  • Harappan urbanism featured planned streets, drainage, craft specialisation, long-distance trade and standardised weights; its script remains undeciphered.
  • The sixth century BCE saw urban growth, territorial states and heterodox traditions. Buddhism’s Four Noble Truths diagnose suffering and prescribe the Eightfold Path; Jainism stresses right faith, knowledge and conduct.
  • The Mauryan state combined central authority with provincial administration. Ashoka’s dhamma edicts promoted ethical conduct and welfare rather than recording a single doctrinal code.
  • The Gupta period saw important work in literature, mathematics, astronomy and temple architecture; do not flatten the varied regional economy into a single “golden age” claim.

Medieval structures

  • The Delhi Sultanate began in 1206. The iqta linked revenue assignment and administration; it was not identical to private ownership.
  • Mughal mansabdari ranked officials and linked rank with military obligation. Akbar’s revenue reforms used measured land and assessed produce under the zabt system in suitable areas.
  • Bhakti and Sufi traditions varied widely but often stressed devotion, moral discipline and a direct spiritual relationship beyond rigid ritual hierarchy.

Colonial rule and nationalism

  • Colonial revenue settlements changed agrarian relations: Permanent Settlement fixed zamindar revenue, Ryotwari dealt with cultivators, and Mahalwari assessed village estates.
  • After the Revolt of 1857, Crown rule replaced East India Company rule in 1858. Nationalism broadened from early constitutional agitation to mass politics.
  • Swadeshi followed the 1905 Bengal partition; Non-Cooperation began in 1920; Civil Disobedience began with the 1930 Salt March; Quit India was launched in August 1942.
Answer frame: context → causes → nature/course → participation → consequences → limitations → historical significance.

Geography

Physical processes · India · human geography

Earth systems

  • Lithospheric plates move over the asthenosphere. Divergent boundaries create crust, convergent boundaries consume or thicken it, and transform boundaries slide laterally.
  • Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion removes and transports it. Rivers erode vertically in youthful upper courses, laterally in plains, and deposit when energy falls.
  • Air rises and cools at low pressure, favouring cloud formation; descending air warms and dries. The Coriolis effect deflects moving air and water right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern.

Indian monsoon and relief

  • The monsoon is shaped by differential land–sea heating, seasonal pressure shifts, migration of the ITCZ, cross-equatorial flow, jet streams, relief and ocean-atmosphere conditions.
  • The Himalaya is a young fold mountain system. The Northern Plains are largely alluvial; Peninsular India is an older, more stable block; coastal plains differ in width and river form.
  • Western Ghats force moisture-laden winds upward, producing a wet windward side and a rain-shadow interior. The Himalaya redirects winds and feeds major perennial rivers.

Resources and people

  • Soil formation depends on parent material, relief, climate, organisms and time. Alluvial, black, red and laterite soils differ in origin and management needs.
  • Urbanisation can raise productivity through agglomeration but strains housing, transport, water and waste systems when planning lags.
Diagram habit: draw cause-and-effect arrows for monsoon, cyclones, earthquakes, river profiles and urban heat islands.

Economy

Macro basics · banking · public finance · development

Output, prices and jobs

  • GDP measures final goods and services produced within domestic territory. Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP removes price change through a base-year measure.
  • Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, not merely a one-time rise in one item. CPI tracks retail consumption baskets; WPI tracks wholesale goods and excludes services.
  • Unemployment may be open, seasonal, structural, frictional or disguised. Labour-force participation and job quality matter alongside the headline rate.

Money, banking and fiscal policy

  • The repo rate is the rate at which RBI lends short-term funds to banks against eligible collateral. Higher policy rates generally restrain demand, but transmission depends on banking and market conditions.
  • CRR is the share of bank net demand and time liabilities kept as cash with RBI; SLR is maintained in specified liquid assets.
  • Fiscal deficit equals total expenditure minus revenue receipts and non-debt capital receipts. It indicates the government’s gross borrowing requirement, not whether every expenditure is wasteful.

External sector and development

  • The current account records trade in goods and services, income and transfers; financial flows are recorded in the capital/financial side of the balance of payments.
  • Currency depreciation can make exports cheaper and imports dearer, but trade response depends on demand elasticity, supply capacity and imported inputs.
  • Inclusive growth combines output with productive employment, access to services, social mobility, resilience and fair opportunity.
Policy analysis: objective → instrument → transmission channel → winners/losers → risks → safeguards.

Environment

Ecology · biodiversity · pollution · climate

Ecology foundations

  • An ecosystem contains biotic communities and their abiotic environment. Energy flows one way through trophic levels; nutrients cycle through biogeochemical processes.
  • Primary succession starts on a surface lacking soil; secondary succession begins after disturbance where soil or biological legacies remain.
  • Food webs are more realistic than single food chains. Biomagnification is the increasing concentration of persistent substances at higher trophic levels.

Biodiversity and protection

  • Biodiversity spans genetic, species and ecosystem diversity. Endemic means geographically restricted; endangered describes extinction risk—neither term implies the other.
  • National parks and wildlife sanctuaries are protected-area categories under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972; conservation and community reserves provide additional approaches.
  • In-situ conservation protects species in natural habitats; ex-situ conservation includes seed banks, botanical gardens and captive breeding.

Climate and pollution

  • The greenhouse effect is natural; human-added greenhouse gases strengthen it. Mitigation cuts causes, adaptation reduces harm, and climate finance supports action.
  • The UNFCCC provides the framework; the Paris Agreement seeks to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue efforts toward 1.5°C through nationally determined contributions.
  • Primary pollutants are emitted directly; secondary pollutants form in the atmosphere. Eutrophication follows nutrient enrichment and can deplete dissolved oxygen.
Species question: habitat → range → ecological role → threat → legal status → conservation intervention.

Science & Technology

Biotech · space · digital · emerging technology

Biology and health

  • DNA usually stores hereditary information; RNA performs diverse roles in gene expression. Genes are DNA sequences, while gene expression links genotype to functional products.
  • Vaccines train immune memory without requiring the disease itself. Platforms include live-attenuated, inactivated, protein/subunit, viral-vector and nucleic-acid approaches.
  • CRISPR systems can target genetic sequences for editing. Promise in therapy and agriculture must be weighed against off-target effects, access, biosafety and germline ethics.

Space and computing

  • Low-Earth orbit is useful for Earth observation and low-latency constellations. A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator at roughly 35,786 km and matches Earth’s rotation.
  • Remote sensing records reflected or emitted energy; resolution may be spatial, spectral, temporal or radiometric. Navigation systems use precise timing and trilateration.
  • A semiconductor’s conductivity can be controlled through doping. Integrated circuits place many electronic components on a small substrate; fabrication demands extreme purity and precision.

AI, quantum and cyber security

  • Machine learning learns patterns from data; generative models produce new content from learned distributions. Performance is not the same as truth or reasoning.
  • A qubit can exist in a superposition and become entangled, but measurement yields classical outcomes. Quantum advantage is task-specific, not universal.
  • Cyber security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability. Strong systems combine authentication, least privilege, encryption, patching, backups and incident response.
Tech answer: principle → application → Indian relevance → benefit → risk → governance response.

Art & Culture

Architecture · sculpture · painting · performance

Architecture and sculpture

  • A Buddhist stupa centres on a relic mound and may include the harmika, chhatra, railing and gateways. Rock-cut chaityas are prayer halls; viharas are monastic residences.
  • Nagara temples usually emphasise a curving northern shikhara; Dravida temples use a pyramidal vimana and later developed prominent gateway gopurams. “Vesara” is commonly used for Deccan synthesis, but regional forms are more varied than three boxes suggest.
  • Gandhara sculpture shows Hellenistic and Roman visual influence; Mathura used indigenous traditions and red sandstone, with both centres contributing to early iconic Buddha images.

Painting, music and dance

  • Ajanta murals combine narrative, expressive gesture and Buddhist themes. Mughal ateliers developed refined portraiture and manuscript illustration; Rajput schools often foreground devotional and courtly themes.
  • Hindustani and Carnatic traditions share raga and tala foundations but differ in history, repertoire and performance conventions.
  • The eight widely recognised classical dance forms are Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam, Odissi and Sattriya.

Literary and devotional currents

  • Sangam literature is an early Tamil corpus; classical Sanskrit, Pali, Prakrit, Persian and regional-language traditions illuminate changing patronage and society.
  • Bhakti and Sufi movements were plural, regionally specific traditions. Compare their social bases, language, institutions and ideas rather than presenting one uniform movement.
Culture recall: period → region → patronage → material/form → iconography → distinctive feature → continuity.
TopicCore distinctionExam-ready implication
Article 32 vs 226Supreme Court for Fundamental Rights; High Courts also for other legal rights.High Court writ jurisdiction is wider in subject matter.
FR vs DPSPFundamental Rights are judicially enforceable; Directive Principles are non-justiciable.Constitutional interpretation seeks harmony, not automatic supremacy of one entire part.
Weather vs climateWeather is short-term atmospheric condition; climate is the long-term statistical pattern.A single event does not establish or disprove long-term climate change.
GDP vs GVAGDP at market prices equals GVA plus product taxes minus product subsidies.GVA shows producer-side value addition; GDP captures the market-price aggregate.
Mitigation vs adaptationMitigation limits climate drivers; adaptation reduces exposure and vulnerability.Energy transition is mitigation; heat-action planning is adaptation.
Fundamental vs applied researchFundamental work seeks underlying knowledge; applied work targets a practical problem.A strong innovation system needs both, plus translation and scale-up.

Practice

Retrieve, decide, explain

Practice with explanations

Choose an option before opening your notes. Each answer explains the rule and the trap, so the question becomes revision material.

04C

One attempt per question. Your score is kept only while this page remains open.

0 / 0 answered correctly
Polity · Q1

Which statement best distinguishes Article 226 from Article 32?

Answer: B. Article 32 protects Fundamental Rights through the Supreme Court. High Courts under Article 226 may issue writs for Fundamental Rights and “for any other purpose”, giving them wider subject-matter jurisdiction.
Polity · Q2

Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill, with any recommendations, within:

Answer: C. Under the constitutional Money Bill procedure, Rajya Sabha has 14 days and cannot amend or reject it; Lok Sabha may accept or reject the recommendations.
History · Q3

Arrange these movements chronologically: Swadeshi, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India.

Answer: D. Swadeshi followed Bengal’s partition in 1905; Non-Cooperation began in 1920; Civil Disobedience in 1930; Quit India in August 1942.
History · Q4

In the Delhi Sultanate, an iqta was primarily:

Answer: A. An iqta assigned revenue from a territory to an official in return for administrative and military obligations. It should not be confused with unrestricted private ownership.
Geography · Q5

Why does a rain-shadow region commonly form leeward of a mountain barrier?

Answer: B. Moist air rises, cools and rains on the windward slope. The drier air then descends leeward, warms adiabatically and lowers relative humidity.
Geography · Q6

Which current is an eastern-boundary current associated with cool water and coastal upwelling?

Answer: C. The Peru Current flows northward along western South America. Cool upwelled water supports rich fisheries and helps reinforce coastal aridity.
Economy · Q7

Fiscal deficit is best described as:

Answer: A. This gap broadly represents the government’s gross borrowing requirement. Its quality depends on why borrowing occurs and what expenditure creates.
Economy · Q8

Which item is recorded in the current account of the balance of payments?

Answer: D. The current account includes trade in goods and services, income and transfers. Investment and borrowing are financial flows.
Environment · Q9

Which process describes a persistent pollutant becoming more concentrated at higher trophic levels?

Answer: C. Biomagnification raises concentration across trophic levels. Bioaccumulation, by contrast, describes build-up within an organism over time.
Environment · Q10

Which pairing is correct?

Answer: B. Adaptation reduces exposure or vulnerability; mitigation limits the causes of climate change. Some interventions can contribute to both, but the core distinction remains.
Sci-Tech · Q11

A geostationary satellite must:

Answer: D. A circular equatorial orbit in Earth’s rotational direction, at roughly 35,786 km altitude, makes the satellite appear fixed over one longitude.
Sci-Tech · Q12

In cyber security, the CIA triad refers to:

Answer: A. Confidentiality limits unauthorised disclosure, integrity protects accuracy and completeness, and availability keeps systems and data usable when needed.
Art & Culture · Q13

Which architectural pairing is correct?

Answer: C. Rock-cut chaityas are worship or prayer halls, often with a stupa; viharas house monastic communities.
Art & Culture · Q14

Which one is not among the eight widely recognised classical dance forms of India?

Answer: B. Chhau is a major traditional dance form but is not in the standard list of eight classical forms. Sattriya, Mohiniyattam and Manipuri are.
GS II · 150 words“Constitutional status does not itself guarantee effective local self-government.” Discuss through functions, finances and functionaries.
GS I · 250 wordsExplain how colonial land-revenue arrangements altered agrarian relations and political mobilisation.
GS I · 150 wordsShow how relief and pressure systems together shape the spatial pattern of the Indian monsoon.
GS III · 250 wordsWhy can a higher policy rate reduce inflation yet create uneven effects across households and firms?
GS III · 150 wordsDifferentiate climate mitigation and adaptation, then give two interventions that create co-benefits.
GS III · 150 wordsAI performance is not equivalent to truth. Examine the implications for public-service use.
GS I · 150 wordsCompare Nagara and Dravida temple forms without treating either as a rigid, uniform style.
Self-checkUnderline the directive, make a 30-second outline, use one diagram or example, and reserve the final minute for a direct conclusion.
Polity · Q15

The languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution number:

Answer: C. The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages. Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali were added by the 92nd Amendment, 2003.
Polity · Q16

The minimum age for membership of the Rajya Sabha is:

Answer: B. Article 84 requires 30 years for the Rajya Sabha and 25 years for the Lok Sabha.
Polity · Q17

The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) is chiefly associated with:

Answer: A. It inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6–14; the RTE Act, 2009 followed.
Polity · Q18

Panchayati Raj institutions received constitutional status through the:

Answer: D. The 73rd Amendment (1992) added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule, giving Panchayats constitutional backing.
Polity · Q19

The Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners are appointed by the:

Answer: B. Under Article 324 the President appoints the CEC and ECs; since 2023 this follows a selection-committee process under the CEC Act.
History · Q20

The Battle of Plassey was fought in:

Answer: A. On 23 June 1757 Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah, opening the path to British political control in Bengal.
History · Q21

The Mauryan Empire was founded by:

Answer: C. Chandragupta Maurya, guided by Chanakya (Kautilya), overthrew the Nandas around 321 BCE.
History · Q22

The Quit India Movement was launched in:

Answer: B. Launched in August 1942 after the failure of the Cripps Mission, with Gandhi’s “Do or Die” call.
History · Q23

The First Buddhist Council was held at:

Answer: D. It met at Rajagriha (Rajgir) soon after the Buddha’s mahaparinirvana, presided over by Mahakassapa with Ajatashatru’s patronage.
History · Q24

The Harappan site known for its dockyard is:

Answer: A. Lothal in Gujarat had a brick dockyard, evidence of the Harappans’ maritime trade.
Geography · Q25

The Tropic of Cancer passes through how many Indian states?

Answer: B. Eight: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.
Geography · Q26

The longest river of India is the:

Answer: C. The Ganga runs about 2,525 km within India. The Brahmaputra is longer overall, but much of its course lies outside India.
Geography · Q27

Anamudi, the highest peak of peninsular India, lies in:

Answer: A. Anamudi (2,695 m) stands in the Western Ghats of Kerala.
Geography · Q28

The first part of India to receive the southwest monsoon is the:

Answer: D. The Arabian Sea branch strikes the Kerala coast around 1 June in a normal year.
Geography · Q29

Black soil (regur) is most suitable for:

Answer: B. Regur retains moisture and is rich in calcium carbonate, making it ideal for cotton; it dominates the Deccan trap region.
Economy · Q30

The Reserve Bank of India was established in:

Answer: C. Established on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934; it was nationalised in 1949.
Economy · Q31

GST, introduced by the 101st Constitutional Amendment, is best described as:

Answer: A. GST is destination-based and dual (CGST + SGST/IGST); it was launched on 1 July 2017.
Economy · Q32

Fiscal deficit is defined as:

Answer: D. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts).
Economy · Q33

NABARD is primarily concerned with:

Answer: B. The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (1982) refinances rural and agricultural credit.
Economy · Q34

Stagflation refers to a situation of:

Answer: A. Persistent inflation alongside stagnant output and unemployment — difficult for monetary policy to fix.
Environment · Q35

The Montreal Protocol (1987) aims to:

Answer: C. It phases out CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances; the Kigali Amendment (2016) added HFCs.
Environment · Q36

Project Tiger was launched in:

Answer: B. Launched in 1973; tiger reserves are administered through the NTCA, statutory since 2006.
Environment · Q37

Kaziranga National Park is best known for the:

Answer: D. Kaziranga in Assam holds the world’s largest population of the Indian one-horned rhinoceros and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Environment · Q38

The Ramsar Convention is concerned with the:

Answer: A. The 1971 convention covers wetlands of international importance; India has 80+ Ramsar sites.
Environment · Q39

The Chipko movement (1973) began in present-day:

Answer: C. It began at Chamoli in present-day Uttarakhand, where villagers hugged trees to stop felling; Sunderlal Bahuguna was its prominent face.
Sci-Tech · Q40

Chandrayaan-3’s landing site on the Moon is named:

Answer: B. Shiv Shakti Point, where India landed on 23 August 2023 — the first landing near the lunar south pole.
Sci-Tech · Q41

The double-helix structure of DNA was proposed by:

Answer: A. In 1953, using Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray data; the Nobel Prize followed in 1962.
Sci-Tech · Q42

ISRO’s Gaganyaan is:

Answer: D. India’s crewed orbital mission, flying on the human-rated LVM3 with the Vyommitra humanoid on test flights.
Sci-Tech · Q43

The SI unit of the power of a lens is the:

Answer: B. The dioptre equals the reciprocal of the focal length in metres.
Sci-Tech · Q44

UPI (Unified Payments Interface) is operated by:

Answer: C. The National Payments Corporation of India operates UPI, launched in 2016.
Convert reading into marks

PYQs and answer writing

Practice is not the last stage of preparation. It is how you discover what to study.

10

The 4-pass PYQ method

  • Pass 1: Sort questions by syllabus micro-topic.
  • Pass 2: Mark recurring themes and the depth demanded.
  • Pass 3: Solve timed; record why each error happened.
  • Pass 4: Reattempt only weak themes after revision.
Prelims error log: concept gap, factual gap, misread question, poor elimination, or reckless guess.

A clear Mains answer

IntroDefine, frame or establish context in 2–3 lines.
BodyUse subheads; cover dimensions, evidence and counterpoint.
CloseGive a balanced, feasible way forward linked to the question.
  • Underline only keywords.
  • Use diagrams when they clarify, not decorate.
  • Answer the directive: discuss, analyse, evaluate, examine.
  • Finish the paper; perfection on one answer loses marks elsewhere.
Compared with leading UPSC platforms

The strongest methods, without the clutter

Drishti IAS, Vision IAS, ClearIAS, InsightsIAS, IASbaba and Vajiram & Ravi differ in format, but their most useful free-study patterns converge.

07
Drishti IASKeeps the full syllabus and exam pattern together, making it easy to check every topic against the official structure.
Vision IASTurns current affairs into a ladder: daily reading, weekly consolidation, monthly revision and exam-stage compilations.
ClearIASDecodes syllabus phrases into study topics and repeatedly links notes back to PYQs and revision.
InsightsIASBuilds consistency through daily answer writing, static quizzes and a named current-affairs source list.
IASbabaUses a practical answer-writing loop: attempt a few questions, compare with a model synopsis, then self-review.
Vajiram & RaviEmphasises PYQ-derived probable themes, concise one-pagers and Yojana/Kurukshetra summaries for revision.

Newspaper triage, not newspaper collection

Cap the first read at about 45–60 minutes. Save only material that maps to the syllabus or strengthens an example.

Daily
The Hindu or Indian ExpressPrioritise explained issues, editorials and national/international pages. Skip party statements, routine crime, local events and repeated facts.
Primary
PIB Features + PRSUse PIB Features for policy background—not every release—and PRS for Bill summaries, legislative context and key provisions.
Selective
Yojana / KurukshetraRead issue-wise for governance, social sector and rural-development examples; make one-page thematic notes rather than monthly transcripts.
Weekly
Compress and testMerge useful items into syllabus notes, write one issue brief, reattempt mistakes and discard duplicate coverage.

Study Plan

A realistic 12-month cycle

Learn, connect, test, revise

Move the start month to fit your target attempt; keep the sequence intact.

06
Months 1–3

Foundation

  • Read syllabus and PYQs
  • Complete core NCERTs
  • Begin polity + modern history
  • Take a timed CSAT diagnostic
Months 4–6

Core coverage

  • Geography, economy, environment
  • Choose optional
  • Make short revision notes
  • Write 3 Mains answers weekly
Months 7–9

Integration

  • GS Mains value addition
  • Finish optional first cycle
  • Sectional tests
  • Essay every two weeks
Months 10–12

Prelims mode

  • Repeated revision cycles
  • Full-length GS-I mocks
  • Timed CSAT every week
  • Error log and elimination practice

The final 30 days: secure, then stretch

Do not start by chasing obscure facts. Protect the high-confidence base, then add differentiators.

  1. Days 30–16 · Revision cycle one: polity, economy basics, modern history, core geography, environment, current-affairs notes and PYQ mistakes.
  2. Days 15–6 · Differentiators: maps, species, reports, schemes, art and culture, science-tech—only from your existing sources.
  3. Days 5–1 · Revision cycle two: condensed notes, marked questions, error log and calm timed recall; no new source.

Targets that create a margin

100+GS Prelims practice target
850+Mains written target / 1,750

These are preparation targets, not official cutoffs or guarantees. Adjust after each full mock.

  • Keep CSAT above the 33% line in repeated timed papers, not just once.
  • If CSAT is weak, give it two fixed sessions every week; recent papers reward preparation.
